::: {.callout-important}
## Collect this brief at the Day 2 morning recap
Forty-five minutes is enough to *build* but not to *decide*. Read your
group's question over lunch, agree on who does what, and arrive at 15:15
ready to type.
:::

## The task

In 45 minutes, produce **one rendered Quarto document** (HTML or Word)
answering your group's question.

Then present it in **four minutes**. Not the code, the finding, and one thing
that surprised you.

## What your document must do

These are the criteria. You are told them now, not afterwards, so you can check
your own work before 16:15.

Met or not met. Nothing is scored, nothing is ranked, and no group is compared
with another.

| | Criterion |
|---|---|
| ☐ | **It renders on someone else's machine.** A facilitator will open your folder and render it. No absolute paths, no files that only exist on your laptop |
| ☐ | **Every number in the prose comes from inline code**, not from typing. At least one visible `` `r ...` `` |
| ☐ | **Missing data are handled deliberately**, with the count stated in the Methods prose |
| ☐ | **One labelled figure**, with a caption that stands alone, and one line saying why that geometry rather than another |
| ☐ | **One `gtsummary` table**, labelled, with one line justifying the comparison you chose |
| ☐ | **Cross-references resolve.** `@tbl-main` and `@fig-main` render as numbers, not as literal text |
| ☐ | **One honest limitation**, naming something these data cannot show |
| ☐ | **An AI disclosure sentence**, or a statement that none was used |

Plus the obvious: a title, your names, and a two-sentence background.

::: {.callout-note}
## What we are not looking at
Statistical sophistication, elegance of code, and whether you found a
significant result. None of those are criteria, so do not spend your 45 minutes
on them.

A group that reports "we found nothing, and here is why our design could not
have detected it" is doing better science than a group that found a p-value
below 0.05 in the fourth subgroup they tried.
:::

## Group questions

::: {.callout-note}
## Group 1: Does attendance explain the effect?
The flipped classroom arm gains more. Is that because of the teaching method,
or because those students attended more?

Compare attendance between arms, then look at whether the gain difference
survives adjustment for attendance. Report both the unadjusted and adjusted
estimates in one table.

*Verbs you will need:* `group_by()`, `summarise()`, `lm()`,
`tbl_regression()`, `tbl_merge()`.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Group 2: Which OSCE stations discriminate?
Using `osce_stations.csv`, find which stations separate strong from weak
students and which do not.

For each station, compute the mean, SD, and the correlation between station
score and OSCE total. A station that correlates poorly with the total is
measuring something else, or nothing.

*Verbs you will need:* `group_by()`, `summarise()`, `left_join()`, `cor()`,
`ggplot2` with `fct_reorder()`.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Group 3: Is burnout related to performance?
Examine the relationship between `burnout_score`, `attendance_pct` and
`posttest`.

Beware the direction of causation: burnout may reduce attendance, attendance
may reduce burnout, or a third factor may drive both. Your document must state
which direction you can and cannot support with these cross-sectional data.

*Verbs you will need:* `filter()`, `mutate()` with `case_when()`,
`ggplot2` with `geom_smooth()`, `tbl_summary()` by `burnout_band`.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Group 4: What do faculty say they need?
Clean `faculty_survey_raw.csv` and describe what it shows about faculty
research practice.

Cleaning is most of the work here: names, duplicates, inconsistent
departments, mixed missing-value codes. Report how many rows you started with,
how many you ended with, and why.

*Verbs you will need:* `janitor::clean_names()`, `distinct()`, `str_trim()`,
`str_to_title()`, `case_when()`, `count()`, `tbl_summary()`.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Group 5: Do the three colleges differ?
The students come from three government medical colleges, in unequal numbers.
Does the college a student attends explain any of the gain, and does it explain
the difference between the two teaching arms?

Start by describing the three colleges: how many students, and are they
comparable at baseline on `admission_score` and `pretest`? Then look at whether
the arm effect holds within each college.

Watch the group sizes. One college contributes fewer students than the others,
and a difference computed on a small stratum is easy to over-read. Say in your
document how confident you are, and why.

*Verbs you will need:* `count()`, `group_by()`, `summarise()`,
`tbl_summary(by = college)`, `ggplot2` with `facet_wrap()`.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Group 6: Do the students who study more do better?
`study_hours` records self-reported weekly study time. Does it predict `gain`,
and does it still predict it once `attendance_pct` is accounted for?

Look at the distribution of `study_hours` before you model anything. It is not
symmetric, and the mean is not a good summary of it. Decide what to do about
that and say what you decided.

Be ready for the answer to be no. A variable that ought to matter and does not
is a real finding, and reporting it honestly is worth more than finding
something in the fourth thing you tried.

*Verbs you will need:* `ggplot2` with `geom_histogram()`, `mutate()`,
`summarise()`, `lm()`, `tbl_regression()`.
:::

## Starter document

Download [`report_template.qmd`](../R/report_template.qmd), or copy this:

````markdown
---
title: "Group N: your question here"
author: "Member A, Member B, Member C"
date: today
format:
  html: {toc: true, embed-resources: true}
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
---

```{{r}}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(gtsummary)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

students <- read_csv("data/meded_students.csv")
osce     <- read_csv("data/osce_stations.csv")
```

## Background

Two sentences: what was studied and why your question matters.

## Methods

Data from 240 students across three colleges (synthetic, for training).
Post-test scores were missing for
`r knitr::inline_expr("sum(is.na(students$posttest))")` students, who were
excluded from analyses of knowledge gain.

## Results

```{{r}}
#| label: tbl-main
#| tbl-cap: "Your table caption."
# your gtsummary table
```

```{{r}}
#| label: fig-main
#| fig-cap: "Your figure caption."
# your ggplot
```

As shown in @tbl-main and @fig-main, ...

## Limitations

One honest paragraph.

## AI disclosure

[Tool] was used to [specific task]. All output was reviewed and verified by
the authors. / No generative AI tools were used in this analysis.
````

`embed-resources: true` bundles images into a single HTML file. You can email
it, and it still works.

## How to split 45 minutes across a group of six

Three pairs, one keyboard each.

| Minutes | Everyone |
|---|---|
| 0–5 | Agree the answer you expect. Write it down. Compare later |
| 5–20 | Pair A writes the analysis code; pair B drafts the prose; pair C builds the table and figure |
| 20–30 | Merge into one `.qmd`. This always takes longer than expected. Nominate who owns the merge before you start, not at minute 20 |
| 30–40 | Render. Fix. Render again |
| 40–45 | Check the eight criteria, decide who presents, rehearse the four minutes once |

The merge is the bottleneck, not the analysis. Give it a person and a deadline.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Render early, render often
Do not write for 40 minutes then render. Render at minute 10 with an empty
skeleton, and again every few minutes. A document that has never rendered
will fail at 15:58, and the failure will be a missing bracket.
:::

## Presentations {#presentations}

**16:15 – 17:00.** Four minutes per group, two minutes of questions.

Six groups at six minutes is 36 minutes of the 45. Changeover between groups
eats most of what is left, so the four minutes is a real limit, not a target.
Have your document already open on screen before the group ahead of you
finishes.

Cover, in order:

1. Your question, in one sentence.
2. Your answer, in one sentence.
3. Your table or figure, on screen, from your rendered document.
4. What surprised you, or what you could not do.

::: {.callout-note}
## Before you present
Run back through [the eight criteria](#what-your-document-must-do). The one
that catches most groups is the first: your document renders beautifully on
your own laptop and fails on anyone else's, usually because of an absolute path
or a file that was never in the project folder.

Swap laptops with another group and render each other's document. Two minutes,
and it is the only way to find out.
:::

## Then

**Post-test, feedback and valedictory**: SET Team.

Please fill it in honestly, including the parts that did not work. The next
cohort inherits your answers.

## After the workshop

- Everything on this site stays online.
- The repository is public. Fork it, adapt it, run it in your own department.
- Bring your own data to the follow-up session: details circulated by email.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
## The one thing to take away
You will forget the syntax. Everyone does, and it is looked up in seconds.
What should survive is the habit: **one project folder, one script per step,
one source document, and a restart before you believe anything.**
:::
